Designing for the person on the other side of the screen

Error handling and user experience
ISYS2001 Introduction to Business Programming
Curtin University

Last week you built your first Gradio app. This week I want to change the question we ask about it. Not "does it run?" but "can the person I built it for actually use it?"

This is a short introduction to user experience. It is not a design course, and we will not be writing any styling code. What I want is for you to leave with a handful of ideas you can apply to your own project straight away, and a habit of sketching before you code.

Your app works. For you.

You know which file to upload, which button to press, and what the output means. The person you built it for knows none of that.

The happy path is the route through your app where every input is exactly what you expected. Real users rarely stay on it: they click too early, upload the wrong file, or bring data that is messier than your test file.

ISYS2001

When you test your own app, you are the worst possible tester. You wrote it, so you unconsciously avoid everything that breaks it.

A robust app is one that copes when it leaves the happy path. That is partly about code, which we will get to, but first it is about understanding who is on the other side of the screen.

Same task, two experiences

App A
Upload file
sales_march.csv
Submit
Error
What went wrong? Was it my file? Should I try again, or email someone?
App B
Monthly sales export (CSV)
sales_march.csv
Calculate revenue
This file has no "price" column. Check the column headers in row 1, then upload it again.
I know what happened, and I know what to do next.

Both apps run identical calculation code. The difference is entirely in how they treat the user.

Look at these two versions of the same app. The pandas code underneath is identical. App A crashes and Gradio shows a generic red error. App B anticipated the problem and explains it.

Notice the other small differences too. App B labels the upload box with what it actually wants, and the button says what it will do, not just "Submit". None of that is clever code. It is just thinking about the user.

Two terms you will hear a lot

User interface (UI)

The parts of your app someone sees and touches: upload boxes, buttons, labels, tabs, messages.

User experience (UX)

Whether they can get their task done, and how it feels along the way, including when something goes wrong.

Think of a café. The UI is the surface you see, like the art on your coffee. The UX is everything from walking up to the counter to leaving with the coffee you wanted, without having to ask three times.

People often use these interchangeably, so it is worth separating them. The interface is the stuff on the screen. The experience is the whole interaction, including the moment it goes wrong.

On the left is the latte art: the part you see first, and the part that gets photographed. On the right is the counter, where the actual experience happens: reading the menu, ordering, waiting, and getting the right coffee. Beautiful latte art does not help if you could not work out how to order. In our unit, we care most about the experience, and Gradio takes care of a lot of the interface for us.

Start with the user, not the code

  • Who is using it?
  • What are they trying to get done?
  • What do they already know?

A regional sales manager downloads last month's export from the CRM and needs total revenue before a 9am meeting. They use Excel every day. They have never heard of a DataFrame.

In business settings, your user is usually a colleague, a manager or a client. Rarely another programmer.

Before you think about buttons, answer three questions. Who is using this, what are they trying to achieve, and what do they already know?

Take this sales manager. They are time pressured, they are competent with spreadsheets, and they have no idea what pandas is. Every decision about wording, layout and error messages should be made with someone like this in mind. For your project, write down who your user is in one or two sentences. It will make the rest of the decisions much easier.

Three principles worth remembering

Show what is happening

People should never wonder whether the app is working.

Confirm the file was received. Show a result, or say clearly that there is none.

Prevent, then help people recover

Make the wrong action hard. When something still goes wrong, explain how to fix it.

Only offer .csv files in the file picker. Say which column is missing.

Speak the user's language

Use the words your user uses, not the words Python uses.

Say "price column", not "KeyError". Say "file", not "NoneType".
Adapted from Nielsen, J. (1994). 10 usability heuristics for user interface design. Nielsen Norman Group.

There is a well-known list of ten usability heuristics by Jakob Nielsen. You do not need all ten for this unit. These three cover most of what goes wrong in small business tools.

The middle one is the bridge into this week's code. First, design the app so mistakes are hard to make. Second, when they happen anyway, catch them and explain them. We will look at both.

What a helpful error message contains

What happened
This file has no "price" column.
What to do next
Check the column headers in row 1, then upload it again.
UnhelpfulHelpful
ErrorPlease upload a file before clicking "Calculate revenue".
KeyError: 'price'This file has no "price" column. Check the column headers, then upload it again.
could not convert string to floatSome prices contain text, such as "twelve". Replace them with numbers and try again.

A good error message does two jobs. It says what happened, in plain language, and it says what the person should do next. If you can only manage one, do the second.

Notice that the helpful versions do not apologise and do not blame the user. They are specific and calm. That is the tone to aim for.

How Python lets you catch the problem

When a risky line fails, Python raises an exception. Think of it as an alarm. With no plan, the app stops.

A try block is Plan A. Each except block is a backup plan for one specific alarm.

Put specific exceptions first and the catch-all last. Otherwise the catch-all answers every alarm and your helpful messages never appear.

def calculate_revenue(file_path):
    try:
        # Plan A: read and calculate
        df = pd.read_csv(file_path)
        df["revenue"] = df["quantity"] * df["price"]
        total = df["revenue"].sum()
        return f"Total revenue: ${total:,.2f}"
    except KeyError:
        # Plan B: a column is missing
        return "The file needs quantity and price columns."
    except Exception as e:
        # Plan C: anything we did not anticipate
        return f"Something unexpected went wrong: {e}"

You have seen exceptions before: FileNotFoundError, KeyError, ValueError. Until now they have stopped your code. A try and except block lets you decide what happens instead.

You do not need to memorise exception names. AI is good at that. What you need is to know which situations to plan for, which is why we started with the user.

Better still, prevent the mistake

upload = gr.File(
    label="Monthly sales export (CSV)",
    file_types=[".csv"],
)

region = gr.Textbox(
    label="Region",
    placeholder="e.g. Perth Metro",
    info="Use the region names from the CRM",
)

Gradio components have settings that do UX work for you. A clear label says what is wanted. file_types limits the file picker. placeholder and info show an example and a hint.

A file picker that only offers .csv files is a convenience, not a guarantee. A renamed file or messy data can still get through, so keep your try and except.

The cheapest error to handle is the one that never happens. Before you write more except blocks, ask whether the interface itself could stop the mistake.

Labels, hints and placeholders take one line each. They also make the app easier to use for everyone, not just people who would have made a mistake. But interface limits are not a substitute for validation in your code. You need both.

Sketch before you code

A wireframe shows what is on a screen and where it sits. No colour, no fonts, no real content. Boxes with a cross stand for images.

Changing a sketch costs seconds. Changing finished code costs hours.

Look at this one. What decisions has the designer already made?

Here is a typical low-fidelity wireframe. Pause and ask yourself what has already been decided. There is a product name at the top, so that is the most important thing. The image sits beside the description, not below it. The detail is split into four tabs, so the designer expects most people to read only the overview.

All of those are user experience decisions, and none of them needed code. Keep an eye on that row of tabs, because it comes back when we look at Gradio layouts.

How screens connect

A screen inventory lays every screen side by side, so you can see what each one is for and what repeats.

Most apps in this unit have one to three screens, or a few tabs. Laying them out still shows you what each one is for.

When an app has more than one screen, it helps to lay them all out together. Notice that every screen here has the same navigation bar at the bottom. Consistency like that is how people learn their way around.

Your projects are much smaller than this. Even so, listing your screens or tabs side by side is a quick way to spot one that has no clear job.

Following one user's path

A user flow follows one person through one task. Each arrow is an action, and each box is what they see next.

Flows can also sit on top of wireframes. Here the arrow shows what happens after "I'm interested": a form opens, and the designer has marked which fields are optional.

A screen inventory shows what exists. A user flow shows how someone moves through it. On the left, the designer has numbered every step a person takes to read and reply to a message, including the branch where they choose between a voice reply and a template.

On the right is the same idea drawn more roughly, on top of a wireframe. You do not need polished diagrams. Boxes, arrows and a few words are enough. The test is simple: can you trace the path from opening your app to finishing the task, and does every step make sense to your user?

From sketch to Gradio

with gr.Blocks() as demo:
1 gr.Markdown("# Sales revenue checker")
2 upload = gr.File(label="Sales export (CSV)",
file_types=[".csv"])
3 run = gr.Button("Calculate revenue")
4 result = gr.Textbox(label="Result")
5 download = gr.File(label="Processed file")
run.click(process_sales, inputs=upload,
outputs=[result, download])

Each box in the sketch becomes one line of Gradio. If you have sketched the screen, you already know what to ask AI for.

Here is a small sales app, sketched first. Five boxes: a title, an upload area, a button, a place for the result, and a place to download the processed file.

Now look at the code. Every numbered box in the sketch maps to one line. The last line connects the button to your function. This is why sketching is not a detour. It is the plan you hand to AI, and it is how you check whether what AI gives back matches what you intended.

When gr.Interface is not enough

gr.Interface

One function. Inputs on one side, outputs on the other. Gradio chooses the layout.

gr.Blocks

You arrange rows, columns and tabs, and decide what each button does. More code, more control.

with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    with gr.Tab("Upload"):
        ...
    with gr.Tab("Results"):
        ...
    with gr.Tab("Help"):
        ...

Remember the row of tabs in the wireframe? In Gradio, that is gr.Tab.

Last week we used gr.Interface, which is perfect for one function with a few inputs and outputs. As soon as your sketch has more structure, such as separate steps, a help section or several tabs, gr.Blocks is the better fit.

You do not have to switch. Choose based on your sketch. If Interface fits what you drew, keep it simple.

What Gradio writes for you

Every web page is built from three layers. Gradio generates all three from your Python.

We will not write CSS in this unit. It is worth knowing the word, because it is what you would ask AI about if you wanted to change colours or spacing. Gradio accepts it through gr.Blocks(css=...), and offers ready-made themes through theme=.

PythonYour Gradio code: components, layout, functions
Gradio turns this into
HTMLStructure: what is on the page
CSSAppearance: colours, fonts, spacing
JavaScriptBehaviour: what happens when you click

You have built a web app without writing any HTML, CSS or JavaScript. That is what Gradio does for you. It is still worth knowing what those three layers are, so the vocabulary is familiar when you meet it at work or in a later unit.

HTML is the structure, CSS is the look, and JavaScript is the behaviour. If you ever want to restyle your app, CSS is the word to put in your prompt. But that is optional, and it is not what we assess.

Prompting AI with your user in mind

"Add error handling to my code."
"My users are sales managers who know Excel but not Python. Add error handling for: no file uploaded, a file that is not a CSV, missing quantity or price columns, text in numeric columns, and a file with headers but no rows. Each message should say what went wrong and what to do next, in plain language. Limit the file picker to .csv files."

Your job: know the user and what can go wrong.

AI's job: the syntax and the exception names.

The second prompt is better because it carries everything we covered today: who the user is, what can go wrong, what a good message looks like, and a prevention step.

AI cannot know your user. If you leave that out, you get generic messages written for programmers. And because you wrote down the cases, you can check whether AI actually handled every one of them.

Arrow keys to move. N for notes. F for full screen.
